entry.evidence: It is important to understand the mechanisms of the transformation of ISWs at continental slopes and identify “hot spots” of wave energy dissipation.

steps.action: Pose the problem of understanding ISW transformation at continental slopes and locating hot spots of wave energy dissipation.
steps.quote: It is important to understand the mechanisms of the transformation of ISWs at continental slopes and identify “hot spots” of wave energy dissipation.

steps.action: Take up the authors' earlier three-parameter (alpha, beta, gamma) classification of ISW-slope interaction regimes as the framework to apply.
steps.quote: A simple three-dimensional α β γ classification diagram was proposed by to distinguish different regimes of ISW interactions with the shelf-slope topography.

steps.action: Cite field observations of ISW breaking on slopes worldwide and of large ISWs, westward propagation and polarity conversion in the South China Sea.
steps.quote: ISWs breaking over slopes have been observed in many coastal locations worldwide

steps.action: State four objectives: compare the classification with data, identify high-dissipation zones, apply it to a Lufeng-like shelf, and determine energy loss.
steps.quote: (4) to determine energy loss as a result of the transformation of ISWs over the shelf-slope topography

steps.action: Derive the regime boundaries: the turning point beta = 1/alpha from weakly nonlinear theory (cited; confirmed in the authors' earlier Navier-Stokes runs) and beta_br, alpha_br from the Vlasenko and Hutter (2002) breaking criterion, giving four regimes in the alpha-beta-gamma diagram.
steps.quote: four different scenarios of ISW interaction with the shelf-slope topography in a two-layer approximation can be realized

steps.action: Report the earlier comparison (Terletska et al. 2020, Table 1) placing field, laboratory and numerical cases in the diagram's zones.
steps.quote: All data were identified as belonging to the corresponding diagram domain.

steps.action: Take SAR-derived wave amplitudes (10-50 m), thermocline depths (40-65 m) and current speeds for the Lufeng region from published observations to set the idealized case.
steps.quote: Wave amplitudes obtained using synthetic-aperture radar (SAR) images

steps.action: Design nine real-scale runs on an idealized Lufeng shelf-slope (L = 18 km, Hmax = 300 m, two-layer tanh stratification) varying amplitude (20, 50, 100 m) and slope (1, 3, 5 degrees) so that runs fall in different zones (Table 2).
steps.quote: In numerical experiments, we vary the wave amplitudes

steps.action: Run the authors' free-surface nonhydrostatic model with a stratified Smagorinsky closure, sigma coordinates, quasi-2D grid, initialized from DJL solutions computed with the DJLES solver.
steps.quote: The numerical simulations were carried out using a free-surface nonhydrostatic numerical model

steps.action: Use the classification criteria to predict for the alpha = 1, beta = 0.4, gamma = 1 degree run a regime of breaking with polarity change, the turning point at h2 = 50 m and breaking at hbr of about 40 m.
steps.quote: The parameters are α = 1 , β = 0.4 , and γ = 1 ∘ and correspond to the regime of breaking with changing [...]

steps.action: Check the model setup against observations: the simulated propagation speed (about 1.2 m/s) is typical for Lufeng, and the initial density profile is shown against a measured SCS May profile.
steps.quote: [...] propagation velocity is about 1.2 m s - 1 , which is typical for the Lufeng region in the SCS

steps.action: Read the simulated evolution of the 50 m wave: polarity changes at 2 h 30 min and the wave breaks at 2 h 40 min.
steps.quote: first changes its polarity at time t = 2 h 30 min and then breaks at the slope at t = 2 h 40 min

steps.action: Place three gamma = 1 degree runs in the alpha-beta cross-section of the diagram and match their simulated behaviour to the predicted regimes (2, 4 and 3).
steps.quote: The final experiment, exp.3, represents cases in which the ISW breaks on the slope before it passes the changing polarity point.

steps.action: Estimate relative energy loss from the depth-integrated pseudoenergy budget of incident, reflected and transmitted waves and build the loss field over gamma and beta from 85 runs (39 lab-scale and 37 step runs from earlier work, 9 new).
steps.quote: Energy loss from breaking waves was estimated following and from the budget of depth-integrated pseudoenergy.

steps.action: Compare the computed energy loss for the step limit (gamma = 90 degrees) with laboratory measurements by Wessels and Hutter (1996) and Chen (2007).
steps.quote: energy loss for the limiting case of an underwater step when γ = 90 ∘ was compared with the results [...]

steps.action: Keep the dependence of energy loss on beta and gamma: Zone 4 is the most dissipative (up to 55 %), with the same peak shape for 5 to 90 degree slopes as at 90 degrees.
steps.quote: It can be seen that wave transformation in Zone 4 is the most dissipative.

steps.action: Compare energy loss between a real-scale run (alpha = 1, beta = 0.4, gamma = 1 degree) and a lab-scale run (alpha = 1, beta = 0.3, gamma = 1.5 degrees): 62 % versus 57 %.
Apply the classification criteria to SCS shelf bathymetry (amplitude 50 m, mixed layer 50 m) to map the interaction zones and hot spots of breaking.
steps.quote: Figure shows an example of a map with zones corresponding to the different regimes of interaction described above.

steps.action: Conclude that field, laboratory and numerical results agree with the classification, which can identify hot spots of energy dissipation.
steps.quote: The diagram is validated for realistic topography configurations.

end.claim: Relative energy loss of shoaling ISWs depends on the blocking parameter and slope over 0.5-90 degree slopes and -2 < beta < 8, peaking in Zone 4 (breaking with polarity change) at about 55-62 %.

decisive_move.sentence: The pseudoenergy-budget estimate of energy loss across 85 numerical experiments produces the energy-loss field on which the headline claim rests.

gates.evidence: The inherited classification guided the choice of runs spanning its zones (Table 2, §3 ¶2) and gave regime predictions before the runs were read (§3 ¶4), which the simulations could have contradicted (Figure 4, Figure 5). The energy-loss field faces only qualitative comparison with laboratory data at gamma = 90 degrees (§4 ¶5) and one cross-scale comparison (§4 ¶6), with no stated failure criterion. The regime criteria (Eqs. 3-6) were published in 2020 before these runs; no analysis or threshold for energy loss was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Dubreil-Jacotin-Long equation solved with the DJLES spectral solver (MATLAB) for initialization
Smagorinsky subgrid model extended for stratified fluid
Iribarren-number breaker classification by analogy with surface waves
Tank measurements of ISW energy loss over steep obstacles (Wessels and Hutter 1996; Chen 2007)

limits: No review file or discussion was supplied, so only the final-paper sequence is coded; the open-discussion history (NPGD) is not seen. The classification, its criteria and its field validation are inherited from Terletska et al. (2020); 76 of the 85 experiments in the energy-loss field come from earlier work (Terletska et al. 2020; Talipova et al. 2013), only 9 are new. Energy-loss values have no stated uncertainty or resolution, and the text gives a maximum of 55 % (§4 ¶5) while also reporting 62 % for a real-scale run (§4 ¶6), unreconciled. No grid-convergence or sensitivity test of the quasi-2D model, closure, or pycnocline thickness is reported. The expectation of higher dissipation on mild slopes (§4 ¶5) is stated but not tested. The SCS zone map (Figure 7) is an untested prediction (sub-claim status: none), not compared with observed breaking. The sub-claim that the classification agrees with field, lab and numerical data is held at regularity_in_range on inherited evidence plus three new runs. Composition none_fits: the walk applies an inherited classification to set numerical conditions, estimates a quantity, and maps it; there are no rivals (not strong inference), conditions are set, not found (not trace series or nature's repetition), and no forecast is frozen. Inference: experiment outputs are available only on request, so reproduction is not possible from the paper.
